title: Hermeneutics
description: How to read the Bible well. This course introduces the theory and practice of biblical interpretation: the nature of Scripture, the historical-grammatical method, literary context, genre, the history of interpretation from the Fathers to the Reformers, the unity of the canon, and the move from exegesis to application. Students practice interpreting narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, gospel, epistle and apocalyptic texts, and learn to test their readings against the rule of faith and the wider church.

quiz_bank.question: Explain the difference between exegesis and application, and why both matter.
quiz_bank.answer_key: Exegesis determines what the text meant in its original context (author, audience, language, genre); application brings that meaning to bear on present readers' lives and situations. Both matter because application without exegesis distorts the text, while exegesis without application stops short of Scripture's purpose (2 Tim 3:16-17).

quiz_bank.question: Why is no one able to read the Bible 'without interpretation'?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Every reader brings language, culture, assumptions and questions to the text, and every act of understanding involves judging meaning (words, grammar, context, genre). The choice is not whether to interpret but whether to interpret well, self-consciously and faithfully.

quiz_bank.answer_key: Verse divisions were added much later (16th century) and often cut across thoughts; the author's argument or narrative unit is expressed in paragraphs and larger sections, so a verse's meaning depends on the flow of thought around it.

quiz_bank.answer_key: Reading a passage in light of the whole Bible - its place in the story of redemption and alongside other texts on the topic. It guards against isolating a text, lets Scripture interpret Scripture, and helps us see fulfilment in Christ.

quiz_bank.question: What was the 'rule of faith' and how did it function in interpretation?
quiz_bank.answer_key: A summary of the apostolic faith (one God the Creator, Jesus Christ his Son incarnate, crucified, risen, coming again, the Holy Spirit) handed down in the churches; it served as a guide and boundary so that readings contradicting the apostolic faith (e.g. Gnostic ones) were ruled out.

quiz_bank.answer_key: Strength - it read the whole Bible as Christian Scripture pointing to Christ and sought spiritual nourishment. Weakness - it could become arbitrary, detached from the author's meaning and history, making the text say whatever the interpreter wished.

key_terms.definition: Identifying the theological principle in a text that bridges its original situation and ours.
Reading all Scripture in relation to Christ, its fulfilment (Luke 24:44).
'That which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all' - a test of catholic doctrine.
The church as the context in which Scripture is read, tested and applied.

discussion_questions: In Acts 15 the church resolves an interpretive dispute. What roles do Scripture, experience and community play?
What are the dangers of 'spiritualizing' a text, according to Spurgeon? Where might it be legitimate?
How can Christ-centered reading avoid forcing Jesus artificially into every verse?

quiz_bank.question: In Luke 24:44 Jesus says everything written about him must be fulfilled in
options: the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms

quiz_bank.question: James 1:22 urges believers to be
options: doers of the word, and not hearers only

quiz_bank.question: The Vincentian canon defines catholic faith as what has been believed
options: by the majority in each age

quiz_bank.question: At the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), James supports the decision by quoting
Identifying the theological principle that bridges the text's world and ours is sometimes called
Describe the steps you would take to move from a passage's original meaning to faithful present application.
quiz_bank.answer_key: Establish the original meaning (context, genre, grammar, history); identify the theological truth/principle; consider how the passage fits the whole canon and its fulfilment in Christ; note differences and similarities between their situation and ours; then apply concretely to belief, character and action, tested by the wider church.

quiz_bank.question: Why is interpretation a communal task and not merely individual?
quiz_bank.answer_key: The Spirit is given to the church; believers across times and places (tradition, creeds, commentators) help check individual blind spots and errors (Acts 15; Vincent's canon), while Scripture remains the final authority.

lessons.paper_prompt: Write a 1,500-2,000 word exegetical paper on ONE of these passages: Philippians 2:5-11, Genesis 12:1-3, Psalm 51, or Luke 15:11-32. Follow the course method: (1) literary and historical context, (2) genre, (3) structure and flow of thought, (4) key words and grammar, (5) the passage in the canon and in relation to Christ, (6) the history of interpretation (use at least two library sources, cited as Author, Title, section), and (7) application for today. Include a clear thesis stating the passage's main point.
